title: Linear-size circuits for integer multiplication
formal: Do there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(n_{0}\ge 1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}, a\) Boolean circuit of at most Cn gates maps every pair of n-bit unsigned integers to all 2n bits of their exact product?
definitions: The circuit has input bits \(a_{0},\ldots ,a_{n- 1},b_{0},\ldots ,b_{n- 1}\), representing \(a=\sum_{i}a_{i}2^{i}\) and \(b=\sum_{i}b_{i}2^{i}\), and output bits \(c_{0},\ldots ,c_{2n- 1}\) satisfying \(\sum_{j}c_{j}2\)ʲ=ab. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; constants 0 and 1 are allowed. Size counts gates, excluding input nodes and output wires. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted. There is one circuit for each n, with no uniformity requirement on how these circuits are generated. Every input must be answered exactly, with no randomness. Leading zeros are permitted. Let \(M(n)\) be the minimum gate count in this model; the proposition is \(M(n)=O(n)\). Changing to any other fixed functionally complete bounded-fan-in Boolean basis changes size by only a constant factor.
answer_criterion: Prove the quantified linear-size upper bound, or prove its negation: for every C and every \(n_{0}\) there is \(n\ge n_{0}\) with \(M(n)>Cn\). A lower bound \(c\cdot n\) with fixed c, a lower bound for bounded depth or restricted wiring, or a limitation of a particular multiplication algorithm does not give the required negative answer. A uniform linear-bit-time algorithm would imply the upper bound, but is a stronger demand than the existence of these nonuniform circuits.

context_blocks.text: Addition admits circuits whose gate count grows linearly with the input width. Multiplication is another elementary arithmetic operation, but the corresponding linear-size bound remains unknown. Goldreich singles it out immediately after the general challenge of proving a superlinear Boolean-circuit lower bound for an explicit function.

The circuit computes every output bit, including carries and the most significant half of the product. Treating a multiplication instruction on a whole machine word as one operation would hide the work being measured. The target concerns exact Boolean computation at individual-bit granularity.

Viola’s author manuscript, carrying a 2023–2026 revision notice, explicitly retains the linear-size multiplication question in Section 4.2. It also proves that multiplication and squaring are equivalent for this linear-size threshold: multiplication gives squaring immediately, and the converse uses squares together with linear-size addition and subtraction.

A negative answer would give a superlinear lower bound for a particularly concrete, efficiently computable family of multi-output Boolean functions. It would apply even to circuits tailored separately to each input length. A positive answer would show that the familiar logarithmic overhead of fast multiplication constructions is not necessary in this circuit model.

The existing TCS-7174 asks for optimal time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine. This card asks only about nonuniform gate count. The archived Karatsuba entry TCS-5168 concerns a reversible pebbling tradeoff, and TCS-6494 asks for a particular reduction from matrix transposition; neither is this unrestricted linear-size question.

why: Determine whether multiplication has the same order of Boolean hardware complexity as addition, or provide an explicit superlinear lower bound in the unrestricted circuit model.

importance.reason: A basic arithmetic operation supplies a concrete candidate for a central circuit-lower-bound barrier. The question is explicitly highlighted in Goldreich’s textbook and retained in Viola’s current manuscript; its nonuniform target is distinct from the catalogue’s machine-time question.
